originalGroup.material:
A. Preparing for a first group walk

Joining a group walk can be an enjoyable way to spend a day outdoors. You do not need expensive equipment for every short route, but you do need to understand the particular walk you have chosen. A little preparation makes it easier to enjoy the company and the surroundings.

Read the route description before agreeing to join. The distance is useful, but it is only part of the picture. ____1____ A short route with steep steps may take more effort than a longer level path.

Ask what the group will do about food and water. A café may appear on the map without being open when you arrive. ____2____ Carrying what you need avoids depending on a stop that may not be available.

Try your shoes before the day itself. Even a pair that feels comfortable while you stand can rub after you have walked for an hour. ____3____ It is easier to discover a problem near home than halfway along an unfamiliar route.

Let the leader know about any difficulty that may affect your participation. You do not need to explain private details to the whole group. ____4____ Then the leader can discuss a suitable pace or suggest whether a different walk would be better.

Finally, check the meeting instructions. Some places have several entrances with similar names. ____5____ Arriving at the correct place is a simple beginning, but it saves everyone from starting the walk with an avoidable search.

B. A letter for next year

Last March, our class ____1____ (visit) the small museum inside our school. Among the old ____2____ (photograph), we found a picture of the playground before the new sports hall was built. A guide ____3____ had once studied at the school told us what had changed.

After ____4____ (read) some former students' letters, we decided ____5____ (write) messages for the class that would use our room next year. The teacher gave each of us ____6____ envelope and asked us to describe one ordinary day rather than list our prizes.

I wrote about arriving late after missing a bus. My friend described a lunch when everyone exchanged seats. We worked ____7____ (careful), because we wanted the future readers to understand small things that might otherwise be forgotten.

The box held not only letters ____8____ also a timetable and a drawing of our room. When all the envelopes were ready, the teacher collected ____9____ (they) and placed them in the cupboard.

We left the box for next year's students ____10____ (enjoy). Perhaps some routines would be different by then. We did not expect our letters to describe the whole school, but we hoped they would give another class a few familiar voices to meet.

originalGroup.material:
A. Giving feedback that a writer can use

A friend asks you to read a draft. You notice a confusing paragraph, an effective opening and several small mistakes. Where should you begin? Useful feedback does not require you to rewrite the piece in your own voice. It helps the writer see how another person is reading it.

First, ask what kind of help is needed. A writer still choosing an argument may not benefit from a page full of punctuation corrections. ____1____ Your comments can then respond to the stage the work has reached.

Describe your reading experience before offering a solution. Saying that you lost track of who was speaking identifies a problem. ____2____ The writer may find a better way to clarify the scene than the one you first imagined.

Be specific about what works, too. A general compliment is pleasant but gives little guidance. ____3____ Explain how that example supports the argument, so the writer knows what to preserve during revision.

Distinguish a question from a correction. If you are unsure whether a statement is accurate, mark the uncertainty and suggest checking it. ____4____ Presenting a guess with complete confidence can replace one problem with another.

When you have many comments, identify the most important few. A list in which every point looks equally urgent can make revision feel impossible. ____5____ Feedback succeeds when the writer can use it to make a considered next decision, not when the reader has demonstrated how many faults they can find.

B. The game in the cupboard

During a classroom clear-out, we ____1____ (find) an old board game in a cupboard. Two ____2____ (piece) were missing, and the lid had no picture. However, ____3____ instruction sheet lay beneath the board, folded into a small square.

The rules ____4____ (print) on thin paper, but most of the words were still readable. Our teacher suggested ____5____ (check) the contents against the list before trying to play. We discovered that buttons could replace the two lost counters without changing the rules.

We were interested ____6____ the way the game used cards to move players around the board. One card could help an opponent as well as its owner, so the choices were not as simple ____7____ they first appeared.

At our first attempt, we did not play ____8____ (correct). We had missed a sentence explaining when to return the cards to the box. After reading the whole sheet aloud, we understood why the game had seemed to end too quickly.

The teacher allowed us ____9____ (borrow) it for the lunch break. We made a fresh copy of the instructions and kept the old sheet beside it, rather than throwing it away. The new copy was ____10____ (clear) than the faded original, but the original remained useful whenever we wanted to check that we had not changed a rule.

A. Returning to a difficult piece of music

Learning a piece of music is not always a steady journey from the first bar to the last. A player may improve one passage while another remains uncertain. When progress seems to stop, changing the structure of practice can be more useful than simply adding another hour.

Identify where the difficulty begins. Players often repeat the whole piece, hoping the troublesome section will improve along with the rest. ____1____ Mark the few bars that repeatedly cause hesitation and give them separate attention.

Slow the passage down enough to notice what your hands are doing. If you cannot complete it accurately at that speed, reduce the speed again. ____2____ Repeating an uncontrolled movement quickly gives you little chance to understand it.

Once the section is manageable, include a little of what comes before and after it. ____3____ A passage learned alone may still feel unfamiliar when approached from the previous phrase.
